--- title: "Blocks, Loops, and Functions" engine: knitr --- ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## Learning objectives By the end of this chapter you should be able to: 1. Explain what a block of code is and how curly braces mark one. 2. Use `if` and `else` to run a block only when a test is `TRUE`. 3. Repeat a block with a `while` loop or a `for` loop, and avoid an infinite loop. 4. Decide when you need a loop and when a vectorized function already does the job. 5. Write a function with one or more arguments, a default value, and a return value. 6. Explain why a function's arguments don't change the variables outside it. ::: What is the first virtue of a programmer? Ingenuity? Grit? Devotion to R? Larry Wall, who created the Perl programming language, gave a surprising answer: **laziness**. He meant a particular kind of laziness: refusing to do the same work twice. A lazy programmer writes a piece of code once and reuses it, instead of typing (or copying and pasting) the same steps again and again. This chapter covers the R tools that let you be productively lazy. **Blocks** group lines of code together. `if` statements decide *whether* a block runs, and loops decide *how many times* it runs. **Functions**, which you have been calling since Chapter 2, give a block a name so you can run it again with new inputs. ## Blocks group lines of code {#sec-blocks} A **block** is the code between a pair of curly braces, `{ }`. R reads everything from the opening brace to the matching closing brace and treats it as one unit: ```{webr-r} { x <- 5 y <- x * 2 print(y) } ``` All three lines run together, and R prints 10. On their own, braces don't change much. Their power comes when you attach them to an `if`, a loop, or a function, which decide whether, or how many times, the block runs. A block either runs completely or is skipped completely. Two habits make blocks easy to read: - **Indent** the lines inside a block by two spaces. RStudio does this for you when you press Enter after a `{`. The indentation shows at a glance where a block starts and ends. - **Check your braces.** Every `{` needs a matching `}`. A missing closing brace is one of the most common errors in R. When it happens, the Console shows a `+` prompt, because R is waiting for the rest of the block. Press Esc to start again. The most common blocks are `if` statements, `while` loops, `for` loops, and functions. We'll take them in that order. ## if statements run a block only when a test is TRUE {#sec-if} An **if statement** has two parts: a **test** in parentheses and a block in braces. R works out the test. If it is `TRUE`, the block runs. If it is `FALSE`, R skips the whole block. ```r if (test) { # runs only when test is TRUE } ``` Before you run the code below, predict the value of `x` at the end: ```{webr-r} x <- 10 if (x < 100) { x <- x + 1 } if (x < 5) { x <- x - 1 } x ``` `x` starts at 10. Is 10 less than 100? Yes, so the first block runs and `x` becomes 11. Is 11 less than 5? No, so the second block is skipped. `x` ends at 11. ### Adding else Add `else` to give R a second block for when the test is `FALSE`. Exactly one of the two blocks runs: ```{webr-r} x <- 3 if (x < 5) { "small" } else { "big" } ``` You can chain tests with `else if`. R checks them from the top and runs the first block whose test is `TRUE`: ```{webr-r} births <- 2500 if (births < 1000) { "few" } else if (births < 5000) { "some" } else { "many" } ``` ### Writing good tests The test uses the comparison and logical operators from Chapter 4: `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `==`, `!=`, `&`, and `|`. Two mistakes come up again and again: - **`=` is not `==`.** `x = 5` assigns 5 to `x`. To ask "is `x` equal to 5?", write `x == 5`. - **The test must be one `TRUE` or `FALSE`.** `if (c(1, 8) > 5)` is an error, because the test gives two answers, `FALSE TRUE`, and R doesn't know which one to use. To decide something for every element of a vector, use the vectorized `ifelse()` instead: ```{webr-r} births <- c(480, 2500, 21588) ifelse(births < 1000, "few", "not few") ``` ## while loops repeat a block while a test is TRUE {#sec-while} A **while loop** looks like an `if` statement, but instead of running its block once, it goes back to the test after every run. As long as the test is `TRUE`, the block runs again: ```{webr-r} x <- 11 while (x < 100) { x <- x + 1 } x ``` R checks the test (is 11 less than 100?), runs the block (`x` becomes 12), checks the test again, and so on. When `x` reaches 100 the test is `FALSE` and the loop stops, so `x` is 100. ::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"} ## Watch out for infinite loops The block must change something in the test, or the test never becomes `FALSE` and the loop never ends. If R seems stuck, click the red stop sign at the top of RStudio's Console, or press Esc. ::: In practice, R users rarely write `while` loops. A `for` loop, or a function that works on a whole vector at once, is almost always simpler. ## for loops run a block once for each item {#sec-for} A **for loop** doesn't have a `TRUE` or `FALSE` test. Instead, it walks through a vector one item at a time. On each pass, the **loop variable** takes the next item: ```{webr-r} for (county in c("Orange", "Durham", "Wake")) { print(paste(county, "County")) } ``` On the first pass `county` is `"Orange"`, on the second `"Durham"`, and on the third `"Wake"`. After the last item the loop stops on its own, so a `for` loop can't run forever. That makes it safer than a `while` loop. Use a `for` loop when you know what you want to repeat over: a set of files, counties, or years. This loop reads each CSV file in a folder and prints how many rows it has: ```r files <- list.files("data", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE) for (f in files) { d <- read.csv(f) print(nrow(d)) } ``` ### Saving results from a loop `print()` only shows a result. To keep the results, make an empty vector before the loop and fill in one element on each pass. `seq_along()` gives the positions 1, 2, 3, ... of a vector, which makes a good loop variable: ```{webr-r} miles <- c(5, 12, 26.2) km <- numeric(length(miles)) # an empty numeric vector: 0 0 0 for (i in seq_along(miles)) { km[i] <- miles[i] * 1.609 } km ``` ### Do you need a loop? Many R functions are **vectorized**: they already work on every element of a vector at once. The loop above does the same job as one line: ```{webr-r} miles <- c(5, 12, 26.2) miles * 1.609 ``` Before you write a loop, check for a vectorized way to do the job. `x + 1`, `sqrt(x)`, `round(x)`, `ifelse()`, and the dplyr verbs you'll meet in Unit 2 all work on whole vectors or columns. Reach for a loop when there isn't one, such as reading many files or downloading data for many years. ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} ## Think about it Later in the book, Chapter 13 downloads American Community Survey data with tidycensus. How could a `for` loop help you download the same table for 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023, and save each year to its own file? ::: ## Functions name a block so you can reuse it {#sec-functions-blocks} A **function** is a block with a name, inputs, and an output. You have already called many functions, such as `mean()`, `round()`, and `read.csv()`. Now that you know what a block is, you can write your own. Every function has the same parts: ```r name <- function(argument1, argument2) { # the body: a block of code result <- ... result # the last value is the output } ``` - **Name.** You create a function the same way you create any object, with `<-`. - **Arguments.** The inputs, in parentheses after the word `function`. Inside the body they are placeholders for whatever you pass in. - **Body.** The block between the braces. - **Return value.** The value of the last line in the block is what the function returns. You can also write `return(result)` to make it explicit. Here is the smallest useful function, `addSeven()`. Running the first three lines only *creates* the function; nothing is printed. The function runs when you call it: ```{webr-r} addSeven <- function(numbers) { numbers + 7 } addSeven(1) addSeven(c(1, 2, 3)) ``` Because `+` is vectorized, `addSeven(c(1, 2, 3))` returns 8, 9, 10 without a loop. ### A preview: the weighted mean center In Chapter 17 you'll use a function, `meanCenter()`, that finds the weighted mean center of a map layer. You don't need to follow its spatial steps yet, but you can already pick out its parts. Its name is `meanCenter`, its arguments are `layer` and `weights`, its body turns polygons into centroids and takes the weighted mean of their coordinates, and its last line, `mean_center`, is the return value: ```r meanCenter <- function(layer, weights) { # convert the polygons into points points <- st_centroid(layer) # weighted mean of the x and y coordinates mc_x <- weighted.mean(st_coordinates(points)[, 1], weights) mc_y <- weighted.mean(st_coordinates(points)[, 2], weights) # create a point with the same CRS as the input layer mean_center <- st_sfc(st_point(c(mc_x, mc_y))) mean_center <- st_set_crs(mean_center, st_crs(layer)) mean_center } mc_pop <- meanCenter(nc_counties, nc_counties$popE) ``` ### More than one argument, and defaults Separate several arguments with commas. You can give an argument a **default value** with `=`. The function uses the default unless you pass something else: ```{webr-r} toKm <- function(distance, factor = 1.609) { distance * factor } toKm(10) # uses the default: miles to km toKm(10, factor = 0.3048) # feet to meters instead ``` ### Putting blocks inside functions A function's body can hold any block, including `if` statements and loops. A common use is to check the input and stop with a helpful message if it's wrong. `stop()` ends the function with an error: ```{webr-r} addSeven <- function(numbers) { if (!is.numeric(numbers)) { stop("addSeven() needs numbers, not ", class(numbers)) } numbers + 7 } addSeven(c(1, 2, 3)) addSeven("seven") ``` ## A function's arguments are separate from variables outside it {#sec-scope} What do these lines print? Predict, then run them: ```{webr-r} numbers <- 10 addSeven <- function(numbers) { numbers + 7 } addSeven(1) numbers ``` `addSeven(1)` returns 8, and `numbers` is still 10. Inside the function, `numbers` means whatever you passed in, here 1. Each time a function runs, R gives it a fresh, private workspace, called its **local environment**, and throws that workspace away when the function finishes. The `numbers` in your own workspace, the **global environment**, is never touched. This idea, which variables a piece of code can see, is called **scope**. It is why functions are safe to reuse: they don't overwrite your variables unless you save their result with `<-`. If you want to keep what a function returns, assign it: ```{webr-r} numbers <- 10 numbers <- addSeven(numbers) numbers ``` ## Your turn {#sec-your-turn} Each of these only needs the pattern `name <- function(input) { body }`. ```{webr-r} # 1. timesTwo(): double its input. Try it on c(1, 2, 3). # 2. addThis(): two inputs, numbers and amount; add amount to numbers. # 3. countAbove(): count how many values in a vector are above a cutoff, # with a default cutoff of 0. ```
``` r timesTwo <- function(x) { x * 2 } timesTwo(c(1, 2, 3)) # 2 4 6 addThis <- function(numbers, amount) { numbers + amount } addThis(c(1, 2, 3), 10) # 11 12 13 countAbove <- function(values, cutoff = 0) { sum(values > cutoff) } countAbove(c(-2, 5, 0, 8)) # 2 countAbove(c(-2, 5, 0, 8), 6) # 1 ```
## Check your understanding 1. In R, a block of code is marked by: 2. What is `x` after this code runs? `x <- 10; if (x < 100) { x <- x + 1 }; if (x < 5) { x <- x - 1 }` 3. A `while` loop whose block never changes anything in its test will: 4. A `for` loop stops on its own after the last item in its vector. 5. To test whether `x` equals 5 inside an `if`, you write `if (x ___ 5)`. Fill in the blank. 6. Which is the simplest way to add 1 to every element of a numeric vector `x`? 7. A function returns the value of the last line in its body, unless you use `return()` earlier. 8. After `numbers <- 10`, `addSeven <- function(numbers) { numbers + 7 }`, and `addSeven(1)`, what is `numbers`? ## Summary - A **block** is code inside curly braces `{ }` that R runs as one unit. Indent it, and match every `{` with a `}`. - An **if statement** runs its block only when its test is `TRUE`. `else` gives a second block for `FALSE`, and `else if` chains more tests. The test must be one `TRUE` or `FALSE`; use `ifelse()` for a whole vector. - A **while loop** repeats its block while its test is `TRUE`. Something in the block must move the test toward `FALSE`, or the loop never ends. - A **for loop** runs its block once for each item in a vector, then stops. Fill a vector made before the loop to keep the results. - Many R functions are **vectorized**, so check for one before you write a loop. - A **function** is a named block: `name <- function(arguments) { body }`. The last line is the **return value**. Arguments can have **default values**. - A function's arguments live in its own **local environment**, so a function never changes your variables unless you assign its result. ## Exercises 1. **Predict, then run.** Without running it, predict what this prints, then check: `x <- 1; while (x < 50) { x <- x * 2 }; x`. 2. **Grades.** Write a function, `letterGrade(score)`, that uses `if`, `else if`, and `else` to return `"A"` for 90 or more, `"B"` for 80 to 89, `"C"` for 70 to 79, and `"F"` below 70. Why does `letterGrade(c(95, 72))` give an error? Rewrite it with nested `ifelse()` so that it works on a vector. 3. **Loop or not?** Write a `for` loop that converts `c(32, 50, 68, 86, 104)` from degrees Fahrenheit to Celsius, `(f - 32) * 5 / 9`, and stores the results. Then do the same thing in one line without a loop. 4. **Running total.** Use a `for` loop to find the running total of births in `c(1091, 487, 3188, 508, 1421)`: the first value, then the first two added up, and so on. Check your answer with `cumsum()`. 5. **Checking inputs.** Add an `if` statement and `stop()` to `toKm()` so that it gives a helpful error when `distance` is negative. 6. **Standard distance again.** (Come back to this one after Chapter 17.) Chapter 17's `standardDistance(x, y)` function returns the standard distance of a set of points. Add a check that `x` and `y` are the same length, and stop with a message if they aren't. ## Further reading - *R for Data Science* (2nd ed.), by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund, free at . The "Functions" and "Iteration" chapters show more ways to write functions and to avoid loops. - *Hands-On Programming with R*, by Garrett Grolemund, free at . Its chapters on `if` and `else`, loops, and environments go further into the ideas in this chapter. - *Programming Perl* (3rd ed.), by Larry Wall, Tom Christiansen, and Jon Orwant (O'Reilly, 2000), where Wall describes the three virtues of a programmer: laziness, impatience, and hubris.
